content: The abdominal examination is a critical component of a physical examination, particularly when a patient presents with abdominal pain or a history suggestive of abdominal pathology. The examination is conducted systematically and includes the following components: setting and preparation, inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation. Setting and Preparation The patient should be positioned supine on a flat examination table. Their hands should rest at their sides, and their head should be supported by a pillow to prevent neck flexion, which can tense the abdominal musculature and hinder the examination. To further relax the abdomen, the patient may bend their knees so that the soles of their feet rest on the table. Proper lighting is essential to ensure optimal visualization, and the patient should be draped appropriately to expose the area from the pubic symphysis to the costal margin. In women, exposure may extend just below the breasts. Some surgeons advocate for examining the abdomen from the nipples to the knees. Concerns about administering pain medications during acute abdominal pain potentially masking diagnostic findings have been refuted by systematic reviews from the Cochrane Collaboration and the Rational Clinical Examination. Inspection The abdomen should be inspected for masses, scars, lesions, signs of trauma, bulging flanks, and abdominal distension. This is best performed from the foot of the bed. Additional findings to assess include jaundice or scleral icterus. Stigmata of Liver Disease Specific signs of liver disease to look for include: Spider angiomas Temporal wasting Fetor hepaticus Clubbing Thenar wasting Dupuytren's contracture Palmar erythema Spider nevi Testicular atrophy Gynecomastia Hematochezia (blood in stool) Hematemesis Gastric bleeding or esophageal varices Caput medusae (rare) Venous distension Ascites Auscultation Auscultation is often performed before percussion and palpation to avoid disturbing the intestines, which could alter bowel sounds. It is also the least invasive and least painful part of the examination, making it ideal to perform first, especially in patients with peritonitis who may become uncooperative after more invasive maneuvers. The diaphragm of the stethoscope should be pre-warmed by rubbing it on the examiner's clothing. Auscultation should be conducted in all four quadrants, though bowel sounds are not strictly compartmentalized and can often be heard throughout the abdomen. To confirm the absence of bowel sounds, one must listen for a full five minutes. Growling sounds may indicate obstruction, while the absence of sounds may suggest peritonitis. Percussion Percussion should be performed systematically across all nine abdominal regions. The liver is percussed from the right iliac region to the right hypochondrium, while the spleen is percussed from the right iliac region to the left hypochondrium and from the left iliac region to the left hypochondrium. Examination of the spleen may involve assessing Castell's sign or Traube's space. Palpation Palpation is conducted in all nine abdominal regions, beginning with light palpation followed by deep palpation. During light palpation, any palpable masses should be noted. Deep palpation is used to further evaluate masses identified during light palpation and to assess the liver and spleen. The most painful area should be palpated last. Muscle tone is assessed by pressing a hand against the abdominal wall, with three pathological reactions to note: Guarding: Voluntary contraction of muscles in response to pressure. Rigidity: Involuntary stiffness of the abdominal wall, indicative of peritoneal inflammation. Rebound tenderness: Pain elicited upon the release of pressure, suggestive of peritoneal irritation. Other Examinations A digital rectal examination is an essential component of a complete abdominal examination. A pelvic examination should be performed only if clinically indicated.
